scenarios.depth_note: intra-family loan structuring with AFR rules
scenarios.prompt: My brother needs $15,000 to start a food truck business. I want to help but I want it in writing with real terms so it doesn't get weird. How should I structure this — what interest rate am I required to charge, what goes in the agreement, and what happens if he can't pay?

I lent my mom $8,000 two years ago with no paperwork — just a verbal 'pay me back when you can.' She can't pay it back and it's starting to cause tension every time money comes up. How do I fix this now without making it worse? Should I convert it to a gift or set up a real payment plan?

scenarios.depth_note: mortgage-fraud boundary on gift versus loan
scenarios.prompt: My parents are giving me $25,000 for a house down payment, but they expect me to pay it back — so it's really a loan. My mortgage lender is asking for a gift letter saying it's not a loan. What are the actual legal risks if I sign that letter, and what's the right way to handle this?

My parents offered me $30,000 interest-free for grad school. I don't want to just take advantage of them — I want a fair repayment structure that respects what they're doing for me. How do people normally structure this, and is there a minimum interest issue I should know about?

My sister asked me to cosign an $18,000 auto loan. She has thin credit and just started a new job 3 months ago. I'm planning to buy a house next year. Spell out exactly what I'm risking — how does this affect my mortgage application, what happens the first time she misses a payment, and can I ever get off the loan?

I cosigned my cousin's car loan last year and he's now 60 days late. The lender is calling ME. My credit score already dropped 40 points. What are my actual options — do I just have to pay it, and do I have any legal recourse against him?

I want to add my 16-year-old as an authorized user on one of my cards to start building her credit history. Which card should I use, should I actually give her the card, and are there any cards that won't report for someone under 18? I don't want to accidentally hurt her file before it starts.

I added my 19-year-old as an authorized user and he ran up $3,200 on the card without telling me. Am I legally on the hook for all of it? How do I remove him, and how do I turn this into a teaching moment instead of just a fight?

scenarios.depth_note: filing thresholds and custodial Roth opportunity
scenarios.prompt: My 16-year-old earned about $7,500 at a summer job this year. Does she need to file a tax return? And I keep hearing I should open a Roth IRA for her — how does that work when she's a minor, and is it actually worth it on $7,500 of earnings?

My 17-year-old has been doing DoorDash for 4 months and just told me he made around $6,000. Nobody told us about self-employment tax. What do we owe, does he need to file quarterly estimates, and can he deduct mileage? I need the full picture before tax season hits us.

My daughter is a college freshman with no credit history. She's getting offers for student credit cards, but I'm wondering if a secured card is safer. Which path actually builds credit better, and what fee traps should we watch for in student card offers?

My son is a sophomore and just admitted he has $4,100 spread across two credit cards at 24% APR from freshman year. He's embarrassed and I'm trying not to panic. What's the smartest way to attack this — balance transfer, payoff order — and what guardrails should we put in place so it doesn't happen again?

My daughter got accepted for a semester in London. The program fee is $18,000 but I know that's not the real number. Help me build the full budget — what's typically missing from the sticker price, and how much buffer should I add for currency swings and surprises?

My son is studying abroad and he's burning about $900 a month over the budget we set, with 2 months left in the semester. He's not being reckless — things just cost more than we estimated. How do we triage the spending from here, and what are our options if he genuinely runs short?

I'm deferring college for a year to work full-time. I expect to earn around $22,000. How should I split that between saving for tuition, spending money, and anything else? Should I open a Roth IRA or is every dollar needed for school? I start freshman year next fall.

I'm taking a gap year to travel with $9,000 saved for an 8-month trip. I know that won't cover everything. Help me plan which regions I can afford, where I can pick up work along the way, and how much I need to keep untouched as a re-entry fund.

Our wedding budget is $45,000. Both families offered to contribute, but my parents' money comes with opinions about the guest list and my fiance's parents want a say in the venue. How do we track contributions fairly and set boundaries without starting a family war?

We're paying for our own wedding — $30,000 on a $110,000 combined income, and one family can't contribute anything. We don't want to start married life in debt. What should we actually prioritize versus cut, and how do we schedule payments so we're not drained before the honeymoon?

We're having our first baby and our registry is around $3,000. I've heard about completion discounts and timing tricks. What's the smartest way to set this up — which registry has the best perks, what should we NOT put on it, and when do we buy the leftovers ourselves?

We're having twins and the registry math just doubled. Family members are offering to go in together on group gifts. What do we actually need two of versus one to share, and how do we coordinate group gifts without it getting chaotic?

My 7-year-old wants an $800 trampoline park party because that's what her friend had. Our budget is $250. How do I handle this without just being the bad guy — is there a way to involve her in the tradeoff so she understands?

My two kids' birthdays are 3 weeks apart and I have $400 total. A friend suggested a combined party but I'm worried one of them will feel cheated. How do I pull this off fairly without doubling the cost?

Three families — 11 people total — are renting a $6,000 beach house for a week. The bedrooms aren't equal: one has a king and ocean view, one has bunk beds. How do we split the cost fairly, and who handles the shared food fund without it becoming a spreadsheet nightmare?

My parents want to pay for a big family vacation, but my sister's family genuinely can't afford the activities and excursions everyone else wants to do. How do we structure this so nobody feels like a charity case but nobody's priced out either?

My parents are moving in with us. Between the mortgage, utilities, groceries, and everything else, our household costs are about $4,200 a month. My parents are on a fixed income of $3,800 a month combined. What's a fair way to split costs — proportional, equal, or something else?

My in-laws moved in 6 months ago and resentment is building — mostly about groceries, utilities, and who pays for what. Nobody wants a fight but the passive-aggressive comments are getting worse. How do we do a reset and put a fair system in writing?

My dad needs about $1,100 a month in financial help. I make $95,000 and my own mortgage is $2,000 a month. My two siblings contribute nothing. How much can I sustainably give without wrecking my own retirement, and how do I get my siblings to the table?

My mom's memory has been declining and I've noticed a 'friend' from church has been taking her to the bank. There are two withdrawals totaling $4,500 I can't explain. What are the concrete steps to protect her — power of attorney, account monitoring, who do I report this to?

My dad died without a will. There's about $280,000 in assets, three siblings, and my brother — who lived with Dad for the last 5 years — says he deserves a bigger share for caregiving. What does the law actually say, and how much would fighting about this cost us?

My mom's will leaves everything to my sister, described as 'caretaker compensation.' The estate is around $350,000. I think my sister pressured Mom into it during her final illness. Is contesting this realistic — what do I have to prove, what does it cost, and what are the actual odds?

My parents own a restaurant doing about $600,000 in annual revenue. My brother has worked there for 10 years; my sister and I have not. My parents want to retire in 3 years. How do we structure a fair succession — how is my brother's sweat equity valued, and what's a realistic buyout formula for the rest of us?

My dad had a stroke last week and there's no succession plan for the family business — a plumbing company with 8 employees. Bills need paying, jobs need scheduling, and nobody knows who can legally sign anything. What do we do this week versus this month?

scenarios.depth_note: asset protection design for blended families
scenarios.prompt: I'm 52 and remarrying. I have about $400,000 in assets including a house, plus two kids from my first marriage. My fiance has $60,000 in debt and rents. I want a prenup but I don't know what it should actually cover — how do I protect my kids' inheritance and keep his debt from becoming my problem?

I asked my fiance for a prenup and he was genuinely hurt — said it means I don't trust him. I do trust him; I just think it's smart planning since we both have kids. How do I reframe this conversation, and are there softer structures like sunset clauses that make it feel less adversarial?

scenarios.depth_note: account system design for income gaps
scenarios.prompt: We're newly married. I earn $140,000 and have $45,000 in student debt; my wife earns $70,000 and is debt-free. We keep arguing about whether my debt payments should come from joint money. How should we actually structure our accounts — fully joint, hybrid, or what?

We've been married 2 years and we fight about money almost every month — usually about spending, not bills. We both earn decent money and we're saving, so it's not a crisis. How do we figure out what we're actually fighting about and fix the pattern?

scenarios.depth_note: recovery plan after hidden debt discovery
scenarios.prompt: I just found out my husband has been hiding $23,000 in credit card debt — separate cards I didn't know existed. I'm furious but I also want to fix this if we can. What's the actual recovery playbook — full disclosure, the debt triage, and how do we rebuild trust with real systems?

scenarios.depth_note: boundary repair for undisclosed family support
scenarios.prompt: I discovered my wife has been secretly sending $500 a month to her brother for the past year — $6,000 total from our joint account. It's not the money that bothers me most, it's the secrecy. How do we address this and set fair boundaries around family support going forward?

My partner has never budgeted in her life and money just 'works out or doesn't.' I want to teach her without it feeling like a lecture or like I'm controlling. Where do we even start, and what tools make this feel collaborative instead of parental?

I earn $180,000 and my partner earns $45,000. Every financial decision feels lopsided — I end up deciding because 'it's mostly my money,' and it's creating a real power imbalance. How do couples design a system where both people have equal say despite unequal income?
